newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS - March 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS - March 13.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CITY BACKS BID FOR CO-OP ARM

A group of City institutions, led by Schroders, has invested nine million stg to back Lanica Trust director Andrew Regan's attempt to buy Co-Op's non-food business. Regan has set up a special purpose vehicle, called Galileo Group, which has major shareholders from nominee companies representing clients of Schroders, Jupiter Asset Management and Killik & Co. The Co- operative Wholesale society has issued a rebuff to Regan, saying it has no intention of selling its non-food business to him.
-- MORRIS SETTLEMENT PROMISE

Philip Morris, the American tobacco group, has made a public declaration that it is prepared to consider a settlement of the smoking-related litigation it faces. This follows remarks by Martin Broughton, chief executive of BAT Industries, that it would consider any "sensible" deal, although it would not propose the terms. Philip Morris has said it will explore reasonable measures that may be in the best interests of shareholders.
-- REED TARGETS ELECTRONIC PUBLISHING FOR GROWTH

Nigel Stapleton, the chairman of Reed Elsevier, has said the Anglo- Dutch publisher could easily swallow an acquisition of more than one billion stg. He outlined the group's ambition to see profits from electronic publishing grow from 18 percent to 50 percent. Deals in scientific publishing could be difficult for competition reasons and Stapleton suggested that business titles in America were more likely.
THE TIMES
-- POUND FALLS AS OUTPUT DENTS CASE FOR RATE RISE

Figures from the Office of National Statistics show that UK industrial output was unchanged in January but was up 2.4 percent against a year ago. Taking the three months to January, manufacturing was up only 0.3 percent compared with the previous three months, the lowest quarterly rate of growth since August last year. City economists say the figures suggest the strength of domestic demand still outweighs the negative impact of sterling. Also, Howard Davies, deputy governor of the Bank of England, has expressed concern about the pound's strength against the mark.
-- ICELAND PLANS BUYBACK AS PROFITS SLIDE BY 23 PERCENT

Food retailing group Iceland has abandoned hopes of taking the company private after announcing plans to buy back a third of its shares. The buyback scheme will cost 118 million stg and comes as Iceland reports a fall of 23 percent in 1996 profits, reflecting the cost of the supermarket price war. Chairman and chief executive Malcolm Walker said he and finance director Bernard Leigh have been in talks with venture capitalists about a buyout but had been unable to agree financing terms.
-- BARCLAYS SELLS IMRY MINUS ITS 'JEWEL'

Barclays Bank has announcedthat it has sold part of the Imry property portfolio to Dutch fund Rodamco for 249 million stg. The deal will include the Shires shopping centre in Leicester and 14 office buildings, but not the West Quay shopping centre project in Southampton. Barclays intends to release 25 million stg from a 44 million stg provision taken out against its investment in Imry to repay debts of 91 million stg.
THE GUARDIAN
-- KVAERNER LOSES MOD ORDER

Kvaerner has lost a 200 million stg Ministry of Defence order for two Royal Navy oil tankers to VSEL, a rival shipyard. This puts into doubt the future of the Kvaerner Govan shipyard in Clyde and its 1,300 workforce. There likely will be political controversy due to claims that the order creates an effective monopoly for VSEL as a builder of large ships for the MOD, against government competition policy.
-- STOP STALLING ON DEBT RELIEF, IMF IS TOLD

The Treasury select committee has urged the International Monetary Fund to stop stalling on debt relief for the world's poorest countries and has called for greater accountancy from the Fund. The committee is backing Chancellor Kenneth Clarke, one of the main instigators of the 5.2 billion stg debt restructuring package for the most deeply indebted countries, which was endorsed by the IMF and commits the Fund to extending the period of loans and reducing interest rates.
-- MOBILE PHONE FIRMS TO REWRITE CONTRACTS

Seven mobile phone companies, including BT, Cellnet and Motorola, have been forced by the Office of Fair Trading to improve their contract terms. The OFT said it was time to use "plain English" and to "cut out the jargon". Airtime contracts have attracted more complaints than any other type of contract. Agreed changes include the removal of disconnection charges, the right to end a contract if prices go up, and shorter periods for customers wanting to quit.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CITY BONUS BONANZA KEEPS ON ROLLING

Schroders and SBC Warburg, two of the City's leading investment banks, have unveiled big increases in bonus payments. This is fuelling fears that bumper payments may encourage risk- taking of the kind recently criticised by the Bank of England. Schroders said that staff costs rose by 30 percent, half due to the payment of higher bonuses. SBC Warburg said that costs rose by a third due to "performance related compensation".
-- CALL FOR MINIMUM EU TAX ON SAVINGS

Finance ministers in France and Germany have called for a EU-wide minimum tax on financial investments. The UK government opposes the move. French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the EU should agree on a code of good conduct to eliminate the risk of unfair competition between member states for tax revenues. The French, German and Belgian governments are concerned about the differences between taxes on capital in EU countries.
-- UNIONS' COMPANY HIT LIST BANKS ON LABOUR WIN

Union officials are drawing up a hit list of companies in anticipation of "union-friendly" legislation to be passed by a Labour government. Officials are targeting individual companies and industrial sectors in preparation for the introduction of a law enforcing recognition where more than half of employees vote for it. Already MSF, the white collar union, has announced intentions to organise employees in the North Sea oil industry.
